summary.intent: Prepare the ask-soony supply-chain decision app for a Sunday demo/hackathon: verify the inventory shortfall figure, build routines automation (UI and backend), and get a calm, minimal, phone-first design direction.
summary.outcome: Routines UI and backend were both built and tests pass (214, 20 new), a design canvas was published and then rejected as too cluttered, and the designer was re-briefed for a Sunday-flow, one-decision-at-a-time concept. The 34,800 vs 6,800 discrepancy was traced to the verifier ignoring in-transit deliveries; nothing is committed yet and the fix is pending a decision.

repo: The team verifier computes shortfall without counting deliveries that arrive before the end of packing (Hwaseong's 28,000 cards), so it reports 34,800 where the paper check correctly gives 6,800 (153,200 needed vs 146,400 available).
`npm run build` rewrites web/dist, which the live app on :8000 serves, so building the UI immediately changes the running app.
Design canvas artifacts must be published from a folder inside the project; data/design/ is gitignored and used for this.
Routines UI lives in web/src/components/routines/ (live.ts, Proposals.tsx, PaneHints.tsx, Undo.tsx); App.tsx and other files were on a do-not-touch list.

Routines backend now supports four triggers (decisions, waiting, shipments, replies), trust modes ask/tell/quiet, proposals persisted in routine_proposals.json, undo, and a cached would-handle endpoint (30s).
UI Undo expects `action_id` (fallback `id`) on activity items; backend records chase/ask_status/call in actions.json with an id, so this needed explicit wiring.

code.finding: Added send_followup(to, subject, body, in_reply_to, references), which sends threaded replies only to supplier addresses from profiles via _send_mail_in_thread (faked in tests).

clean_spec rejects nonsensical combos (chase on open decisions, silent_hours outside shipments) with plain reasons used by the editor agent's repair round; supports per-step 'when' so chase-at-2h and call-at-4h fit one routine.
summarise() keeps its signature; summary and facts come from one cached model call; after-launch is decided by comparing the reply date to state['clock']['launch'].

workflow: Delegating UI, backend and design to parallel subagents with explicit contracts and do-not-touch lists worked, but the lead needs to verify cross-agent wiring (e.g. action id exposure) before committing.
Commit UI and backend together so the server and UI never go live out of step.
Screens built as design targets should be reviewed by the user early; the first canvas was rejected for clutter, so a low-cost reduction brief up front would save a round.
Frame UX briefs around a concrete user scenario (Sunday 06:30, phone in hand) to get radical simplification.

friction: User found all three design directions far too cluttered; the designer's first round had to be redone.
Designer's original page A had inconsistencies (overlapping timeline labels, clock not matching deadlines, glyph icons).
Two contradictory cards (34,800 verifier vs 6,800 paper check) in the inbox risk confusing the demo.
The backend's silent_hours is measured against the newest update of any shipment, so a total feed stop reads as 0 hours silent.
DecisionList has no refresh hook, so Undo there only reflects after the next 5s app refresh.
open_items: Decide whether to send Farhan the 34,800 vs 6,800 calculation and whether to build the fallback (paper check card wins over the verifier card for the same part).
Commit and push UI plus backend together once they fit and tests pass; confirm the action id wiring on activity items.
Receive the redesigned minimal Sunday-flow screens (notification, decision, source tapped, done, all clear, desktop focus), put them on the canvas, and then rebuild the real app along that direction.
Apply the chosen design direction to code, including routines, login, PWA icon and Teams card.
Optionally pass onChanged from App to DecisionList for instant undo refresh.
A status-question email has no decision attached, so a supplier's answer won't appear on a card.
Confirm the would-handle response shape ({card_id: [...]}) matches between UI and backend.
